notes: Slot 1 = PDC (Frei), using the MD PDC sprite. Frei's PDC governed alone, so coalition slot 2 holds the opposition Partido Nacional, the main liberal-conservative force. Partido Radical moved to slot 3 (social-democratic turn, starting popularity) with the MD PR sprite; PS kept in MD slot 18; MAPU in 19; MIR in 5.

0.name: Movimiento Gremial
0.text:
The Gremialist Movement was founded in 1967 at the Pontifical Catholic University in Santiago by Jaime Guzmán, then a law student, to fight the reformist takeover of the university. By 1970 it has won control of the Catholic University student federation and become the most disciplined youth cadre of the Chilean right, distrustful of Christian Democrat reformism and of party politics as such.

Gremialismo draws on Catholic corporatism and Spanish traditionalist thought: guilds, professions and universities must be free of partisan politics, while a strong executive guarantees order. Fiercely anti-Marxist and pro-American, it recruits among upper-class students and links naturally to business associations and conservative officers.

1.name: Partido Demócrata Cristiano
1.text:
The Christian Democratic Party has governed Chile since Eduardo Frei Montalva won the presidency in 1964 under the banner of a 'Revolution in Liberty'. Born from the Falange Nacional of the 1930s, it is the largest party in Congress, but the 1969 defection of its left wing to MAPU and Frei's constitutional bar on re-election leave it facing the 1970 contest with Radomiro Tomic as its candidate.

The PDC offers communitarian reform as an alternative to both capitalism and Marxism: agrarian reform, the 'Chileanization' of copper, peasant unions and social housing, backed by the Alliance for Progress. Its base lies in the middle classes, Catholic youth, organized peasants and shantytown associations.

2.name: Partido Nacional
2.text:
The National Party was formed in 1966 when the historic Conservative and Liberal parties, crushed by the Christian Democratic landslide, merged with Jorge Prat's nationalists. Led by Sergio Onofre Jarpa, it recovered strongly in the 1969 parliamentary elections and now backs the independent candidacy of former president Jorge Alessandri for 1970.

The Nationals defend private property, the landed estates threatened by agrarian reform and a firm executive able to restore authority. Staunchly anti-communist and pro-American, they rely on landowners, business, the Santiago upper class and conservative provincial voters, and on Alessandri's personal prestige far beyond party lines.

3.name: Partido Radical
3.text:
The Radical Party, founded in 1863, is the historic party of the Chilean middle class, of teachers, civil servants and freemasons, and led the Popular Front governments of 1938 to 1952. After its congresses swung the party leftwards and its anti-Marxist wing walked out in 1969, it has joined the Socialists and Communists in the new Unidad Popular, putting forward Senator Alberto Baltra as a pre-candidate for the presidency.

Increasingly social democratic, the party advocates planning, secular education and a broader welfare state within constitutional limits. Its strength rests on provincial networks, the public sector and the Masonic lodges, making it the moderating bridge between the Marxist left and the centre.

4.name: Partido Comunista de Chile
4.text:
The Communist Party of Chile, founded in 1922 by Luis Emilio Recabarren, is the largest and best-organized communist party in the Americas outside Cuba. Legal again since 1958, it is led by Secretary-General Luis Corvalán and has put forward the poet Pablo Neruda as its presidential pre-candidate while negotiating the common programme of the Unidad Popular.

Loyal to Moscow, the party pursues the 'peaceful road' to socialism through elections, broad alliances and mass unions rather than guerrilla war. Its power rests on the copper and nitrate miners, the CUT trade-union federation, disciplined youth brigades and a solid electoral base in industrial Santiago and the north.

5.name: Movimiento de Izquierda Revolucionaria
5.text:
The Revolutionary Left Movement was founded in Concepción in 1965 by students, Trotskyists and dissident socialists. Since 1967 it has been led by the young physician Miguel Enríquez, and after a wave of bank expropriations in 1969 its leaders have gone underground, hunted by the police.

The MIR rejects the electoral road as an illusion and calls for armed struggle on the Cuban model, organizing land seizures with Mapuche peasants, shantytown takeovers and radical student cells. It distrusts Moscow and the Communist Party alike, admires Havana, and draws its strength from university youth in Concepción and Santiago and from the most marginal urban and rural poor.

6.name: Los del Tacnazo
6.text:
In October 1969 General Roberto Viaux led the Tacna artillery regiment in Santiago into a barracks revolt over pay, equipment and the neglect of the armed forces. The 'Tacnazo' ended in negotiation and Viaux's forced retirement, but it left behind a network of resentful officers and civilian admirers who see him as their leader.

The group mixes professional grievance with a hard nationalist creed: contempt for politicians, suspicion of foreign capital and American tutelage alike, and a belief that the army must save the nation from decadence. It has little popular following, but its contacts inside the barracks and among ultra-right activists make it a constant conspiratorial danger.

7.name: Ejército de Liberación Nacional
7.text:
The Chilean National Liberation Army is a clandestine network formed in 1967 inside the Socialist Party to support Che Guevara's guerrilla in Bolivia. Led by Elmo Catalán, with Beatriz Allende among its key organizers, it smuggled survivors of the Bolivian campaign to safety and keeps close ties to the Cuban intelligence services.

Its members believe socialism will be won by a disciplined revolutionary vanguard and a strong state on the Cuban model rather than by parliamentary majorities. Small but well connected, it operates as Havana's arm within the Chilean left, providing safe houses, training contacts and couriers for continental insurgency.

8.name: Los Amigos de Musa Sadr
8.text:
A small circle of Lebanese Shia emigrants in Santiago and the northern free port of Arica follows the rise of Imam Musa al-Sadr, who in 1969 became chairman of the new Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Lebanon. Remittances, letters and visiting relatives tie them closely to the villages of southern Lebanon.

The circle favours a socially engaged, reformist Shia Islam that demands dignity and development for the poor without rejecting coexistence with Christians. In Chile it keeps a low profile within a mostly Christian Arab colony, organizing prayer, charity and Arabic lessons, and its influence rests on merchant families rather than any political organization.

9.name: Círculo de Nayaf
9.text:
A handful of young Shia students and traders of Lebanese origin in Santiago read the sermons smuggled out of Najaf, where the exiled Iranian cleric Ruhollah Khomeini teaches that Islamic jurists must rule the state. They meet privately and correspond with seminary students in Iraq and Lebanon.

The circle rejects both Western capitalism and atheist communism and dreams of a revolutionary order guided by a supreme jurist. It has no public presence and only a few dozen sympathizers, but its members' ties to the wider Lebanese diaspora across South America give it a reach beyond its size.

10.name: Sociedad Unión Musulmana de Chile
10.text:
The Muslim Union Society, founded in Santiago in 1926 by Syrian and Palestinian immigrants, is the oldest Islamic institution in Chile. It represents a few hundred families within a largely Christian Arab community and has long sought land and funds for a proper mosque.

The society embraces an establishment, apolitical Islam: prayer, Arabic instruction, burials and charity under the patronage of wealthy merchants, with cordial ties to the Chilean state. Increasingly it looks to Saudi Arabia and the Muslim World League for books, imams and money, giving conservative Gulf-oriented teachings a foothold among Chilean Muslims.

11.name: Células del Tahrir
11.text:
A few Palestinian and Syrian students at Santiago's universities have come into contact with Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani. Through pamphlets from Beirut and Amman they form tiny study cells that debate the restoration of the caliphate.

The cells reject nationalism, democracy and the Arab regimes alike and see the 1967 defeat as proof that only a united Islamic state can liberate Palestine. They have no following among the established Arab colony, whose leaders regard them as dangerous, but they cultivate disaffected youth through prayer rooms and student societies.

12.name: Juventud Musulmana de Santiago
12.text:
Muslim Youth of Santiago is a loose association of young Muslims, mostly children of Syrian and Palestinian immigrants and a few Chilean converts, who gather around the Muslim Union Society. Its members read Hassan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb in Arabic and in French translations reaching them via Buenos Aires.

It calls for an Islamic revival combining piety, education and social work, inspired by the Muslim Brotherhood. Hostile to Zionism and critical of both superpowers, it seeks to defend Muslim identity in a Catholic society, but its influence remains limited to a few dozen activists and their families.

13.name: Corporación de Fomento de la Producción
13.native_full: Corporación de Fomento de la Producción
13.text:
The Production Development Corporation, created in 1939 by the Popular Front government, is the engine of the Chilean state economy. It founded the national steel, electricity and oil companies, and under Frei it finances agro-industry, petrochemicals and the 'Chileanized' copper ventures alongside the national planning office ODEPLAN.

Its engineers and economists, many schooled in the ideas of CEPAL, believe development must be planned by experts above party quarrels. They favour import-substituting industry, state enterprise and credit from any lender willing to pay, and their leverage lies in controlling investment, credit and the technical knowledge every government needs.

14.name: Democracia Radical
14.text:
Radical Democracy was founded in 1969 by Senator Julio Durán and other right-wing Radicals who refused their party's alliance with the Socialists and Communists. Durán, the Radical presidential candidate of 1964, takes with him a share of the old party's provincial machine and its anti-Marxist voters.

The party stands for secular, middle-class republicanism, a mixed economy and the Western alliance, but above all for keeping the Marxists out of power. It leans towards Jorge Alessandri's independent candidacy and appeals to civil servants, small proprietors and freemasons alarmed by the Radical Party's leftward drift.

15.name: Sociedad Nacional de Agricultura
15.text:
The National Agriculture Society, founded in 1838, is the guild of Chile's great landowners and one of the oldest employers' organizations in the Americas. Since Frei's agrarian reform law of 1967 began expropriating large estates, it has become the fiercest opponent of the government, flanked by the industrialists of SOFOFA.

The society defends private property, the estate economy of the Central Valley and the political weight of rural notables. It fights expropriations in the courts and the press, funds the National Party and Jorge Alessandri, and relies on long-standing ties to El Mercurio, the bench and the officer corps.

16.name: Los Chicago Boys
16.text:
The 'Chicago Boys' are Chilean economists trained at the University of Chicago under an exchange agreement signed with the Catholic University in 1956. Led by Sergio de Castro, dean of the Catholic University's economics faculty, they have turned the school into a stronghold of monetarist thinking.

They argue that inflation, protectionism and state planning are strangling Chile, and propose free prices, open trade, privatization and a small state. Outside the academy they remain marginal, but they find a ready audience in El Mercurio and the business associations, which gives them a path to influence if the right returns to power.

17.name: Comité Nacional pro Defensa de la Fauna y Flora
17.english: National Committee for the Defence of Fauna and Flora
17.native_full: Comité Nacional pro Defensa de la Fauna y Flora
17.text:
The National Committee for the Defence of Fauna and Flora was founded in 1968 by naturalists, scientists and hunters worried about the destruction of Chile's native forests and wildlife. It is a small volunteer association based in Santiago, but the first of its kind in the country.

CODEFF campaigns for national parks, the protection of species such as the huemul and the vicuña, and limits on the logging and burning of the southern forests. It has no partisan alignment and little money, but its scientific reputation and press campaigns give it a voice with the agriculture ministry and the universities.

18.name: Partido Socialista de Chile
18.text:
The Socialist Party of Chile, founded in 1933 by Marmaduke Grove, Eugenio Matte and Salvador Allende among others, is the larger partner of the Marxist left alongside the Communists. Its 1967 Chillán congress declared revolutionary violence legitimate, yet it remains bound to Senator Salvador Allende, who is seeking the presidency for the fourth time through the Unidad Popular.

Non-aligned and Latin American in outlook, the party admires Cuba and Yugoslavia while keeping its distance from Moscow. It demands the nationalization of copper, banks and big industry and a deep agrarian reform, and draws its strength from industrial workers, miners, intellectuals and the left of the middle class.

19.name: Movimiento de Acción Popular Unitaria
19.text:
The Popular Unitary Action Movement was born in May 1969 when the rebel wing of the Christian Democrats, led by Jacques Chonchol, Rodrigo Ambrosio and Rafael Agustín Gumucio, broke with Frei's government over the pace of reform. Within months it joined the Unidad Popular and named Chonchol as a pre-candidate for the presidency.

MAPU combines Catholic social radicalism with an increasingly Marxist analysis, rejecting both the Soviet model and the Christian Democratic middle way. Its strength lies among agrarian reform technicians, peasant unions, Catholic university youth and young professionals, giving the left a foothold in milieus the old parties never reached.

20.name: Partido Democrático Nacional
20.text:
The National Democratic Party was formed in 1960 by followers of Carlos Ibáñez del Campo, the former dictator and later elected president, uniting several small populist and nationalist groups. Once a significant force in the provinces, it has dwindled since Ibáñez's death, and its factions are now courted by both left and right ahead of 1970.

PADENA promises strong leadership, honest government and protection for small farmers, employees and pensioners against both oligarchs and party machines. Its rhetoric is nationalist and anti-politician, and its remaining leverage lies in personal clienteles in the countryside and a nostalgic electorate still loyal to the memory of the 'General of Hope'.

21.name: Movimiento Revolucionario Nacional Sindicalista
21.text:
The National Syndicalist Revolutionary Movement was founded in 1952 by Ramón Callis, taking its ideas and symbols from José Antonio Primo de Rivera's Spanish Falange. Small and street-oriented, it survives on the margins of Chilean politics through youth groups, uniformed rallies and brawls with leftist students.

The MRNS rejects liberal democracy, capitalism and Marxism alike and calls for a corporatist national-syndicalist state built on Catholic values and Hispanic heritage. Its numbers are tiny, but as the left advances its militants find new sympathy among frightened middle-class youth and some officers, and they stand ready to act as shock troops of the far right.

22.name: Fuerzas Armadas de Chile
22.text:
The Chilean Armed Forces, comprising the army, navy and air force, pride themselves on a record of obedience to civilian rule unbroken since 1932. After the Tacnazo revolt of October 1969 Frei appointed General René Schneider as army commander-in-chief to restore discipline.

Schneider insists that the army must stay out of politics and respect whatever the voters decide in 1970, a stance that frustrates conservative officers. The forces are trained and equipped largely by the United States, deeply anti-communist in culture, and their underpaid officer corps resents politicians, a combination that makes their neutrality less solid than it appears.

23.name: Reino de la Araucanía y la Patagonia
23.native_full: Reino de la Araucanía y la Patagonia
23.text:
The Kingdom of Araucanía and Patagonia was proclaimed in 1860 by the French adventurer Orélie-Antoine de Tounens, who briefly won the backing of Mapuche chiefs before Chilean troops seized him. Its claims are kept alive from France by the pretender Philippe Boiry, styled Prince Philippe of Araucanía and Patagonia.

The royal house presents itself as the protector of Mapuche autonomy and of the lands taken in the 'Pacification of Araucanía'. It has no presence in Chilean politics beyond curiosity, but its symbolism appeals to some Mapuche activists in the south who resent the Chilean state's broken promises.
